title: Awareness, Spontaneity, Intimacy
concept: After this one you can pick the move that is yours in three short moments, not the one you were trained to make.
bookIdea: Berne says autonomy shows up as three recovered capacities: awareness, which is seeing and hearing for yourself in the here and now instead of as you were taught; spontaneity, which is the freedom to choose and show your feelings from the whole range of Parent, Adult and Child instead of only the taught ones; and intimacy, which is game-free candour, and he adds that you start life with all three, lose them to early adaptation, and have to keep winning them back.

opener.setting: Saturday, 10:15am, the balcony, Hawthorn Court, apartment 3B. The sun is already hot on the railings.

lines.text: “Morning, love. Sit down, I've got something for you.”
lines.cue: coming up the step slowly, one hand on the railing, knees creaking

opener.ask: In each of the next three moments, which move is yours, and which one is the script?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Being your own person has three parts. Noticing is seeing and hearing for yourself, here and now, in your own way and without the labels you were handed. Choosing fresh is picking the feeling and the reply you want from all your voices, including the ones you were never taught to use. Being real is plain candour with no game in it.

items.text: “Hang on, Gran. Smell that. It's sharp and cold, and the peel is thick on one side.”
items.cue: peeling the orange, eyes on your thumbs
items.why: You take the orange in with your own senses, here and now, and describe it in your own words instead of saying the polite thing you were taught. That is noticing.

traps.1: Choosing fresh. It sounds like a new reply, but the line only describes the orange. Nothing was picked against a habit.
traps.2: Being real. It is honest, but the line tells her nothing about how you feel. It stays with the orange, which is noticing.

items.example:
Mango stall, by the bus stop, Saturday, 8:00am.
Customer: “These look tired. Is the one at the front fresher?”
Vendor: “Yes. Smell it, you'll see.”

items.text: “Fine is what I always say. Tonight it's starving, and a bit cross, and I want a biscuit before the rice.”
items.cue: to Maya, at the stove, who expected 'fine'
items.why: You catch the usual 'fine' coming and pick a different feeling to show, a hungry, cross, playful one. Choosing which feeling to show, instead of only the taught one, is choosing fresh.

traps.0: Noticing. You do catch the habit, but the work of the line is picking a different feeling to show. Noticing alone would stop at 'I'm about to say fine'.
traps.2: Being real. It is honest, but the heart of the line is the switch from the taught reply to a chosen one. The candour in it comes second.

items.example:
Office lift, Monday, 8:55am.
Colleague: “Good weekend?”
You (who always say “Yes, fine”): “Loud. A wedding, and I'm shattered, and I loved it.”

items.text: “No, Mum, I skip lunch when the deadlines close in. I'm scared the money won't stretch, and I didn't want you to worry.”
items.cue: on the balcony, phone pressed to your ear
items.why: You say the plain thing with no joke, no hint and no hook, and no game in it. That is being real.

traps.0: Noticing. You do notice the deadlines, and that is in the line. But noticing alone stays on the facts, and this line goes on to say how you feel.
traps.1: Choosing fresh. It is a new answer to 'are you eating', but what makes it new is the honesty, so the better name is being real.

items.example:
Sister's WhatsApp, Sunday night.
Sister: “Are you sleeping? Tell me the truth.”
You: “Not well. The baby's cough keeps me up, and I didn't want to say it.”
Sister: “Oh. Now we can talk.”

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Three short scenes. In each one, pick the move that is yours, not the one you were taught.

items.title: Saturday, 10:15am, the balcony
items.setting: Gran has come up the step with a single orange from the morning stall, still cold from the bag.

beats.text: “Eat this orange while it's cold. I walked to the stall for it this morning.”

lines.text: “Thank you, Gran. You shouldn't have gone out.”
lines.outcome: She waves it off. “Walking is good for me,” she says, and sits down on the step.
lines.why: This is the polite script. It is kind, and it skips the orange, which is the thing she actually gave you.

lines.text: “It smells sharp. Did you pick it yourself, or is that the stall's?”
lines.outcome: Gran's face opens. “I picked it. Look, you can see my thumb mark on the skin.”
lines.why: You notice what is actually here, the smell and the thumb mark on the peel. Noticing gives her something real back.

lines.text: “You always do this. Now I owe you, and you'll keep telling me so.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Gran puts the orange on the step and says nothing about it.
lines.why: This turns a gift into a debt. The orange becomes a ledger entry, and she will keep reminding you of the price.

beats.text: “Go on, peel it. Tell me something from the week. I never hear anything.”
beats.cue: watching your hands on the peel

lines.text: “I'm peeling it badly. The demo went well, and I'm a bit proud of it.”
lines.outcome: Gran claps once. “Badly is still an orange,” she says, and leans in for the details.
lines.why: You say how you are, with a small true detail about yourself. It is a fresh line, not the one you would have said at the start of the year.

lines.text: “Nothing much happened this week, Gran.”
lines.outcome: She nods and goes back to her knee, which she describes in full.
lines.why: It is the scripted small talk. That closes the door on the one thing she asked for.

beats.text: “Is it sweet? Tell me it's sweet, or I'll think the stall cheated me.”
beats.cue: laughing at her own joke, one hand on the railing

lines.text: “It's sweet at the back and sharp at the front. A bit like you, Gran.”
lines.outcome: She pats your arm. “Flatterer. Eat the rest, and don't waste the peel.”
lines.why: You notice the taste exactly, and you say one true thing about her. It has warmth in it because it is specific.

lines.text: “It's lovely, Gran. Thank you.”
lines.outcome: She nods, pleased. Then she asks about the knee again.
lines.why: A polite yes that ends the moment. There is nothing wrong with it, and nothing new in it either.

items.payoff: Saturday, 10:40am. The orange goes soft on the step, and Gran brings up the debt at lunch and again at dinner.
items.example:
Sweet shop, by the bus stop, Friday.
Shopkeeper: “Try the fudge, it's on the house. You can owe me a visit.”
You: “Thanks. Which one's the fresh one?”

items.title: Tuesday, 8:20pm, the kitchen
items.setting: Apartment 3B. Maya is at the stove, still in her scrubs. The rice has been on for an hour.

lines.text: “I'm fine, Maya. I'll eat later.”
lines.outcome: Maya says “Fine” back and turns the gas down. The kitchen goes quiet.
lines.why: This is the trained reply. It answers the question and closes the door, so the two of you carry on apart.

lines.text: “No, I haven't. Sit with me for ten minutes while I eat, if you can.”
lines.outcome: Maya turns round, surprised. She pulls out a chair. “Ten minutes. Then I'm back on the rice.”
lines.why: You answer from a fresh place, with the true thing and a request for company. It breaks the old loop, and she gets to be asked for something instead of only doing the cooking.

lines.text: “Sure, Maya. Like you ever sit down for anyone.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Maya stops stirring and says “Right,” then eats standing at the sink, alone.
lines.why: This is a sting dressed up as a reply. It gives her the accusation she has already filed, and nobody sits down.

beats.text: “Okay. Then what's the matter? You look like you're carrying the whole building.”
beats.cue: pulling out the chair, not sitting yet

lines.text: “Nothing serious. Just work.”
lines.outcome: She nods and turns back to the rice.
lines.why: Work is the safe answer, and it keeps the two of you at arm's length.

lines.text: “The bank called about the deposit, and I've been telling everyone it's fine all day.”
lines.outcome: Maya sits down, for the first time all day. “Then it isn't fine. Tell me the number.”
lines.why: You name the word you have been using as a shield, and the real thing under it. Choosing fresh is a line that didn't come from the reflex.

beats.text: “Right. Ten minutes. Tell me the number, and don't make it smaller.”
beats.cue: a plate in each hand now, setting one down for you

lines.text: “It's a big fee, and I told the landlord Friday. I'm not calm about it at all.”
lines.outcome: Maya puts the plate down. “Okay. Friday's a real day. Let's do the sums.”
lines.why: You give the true number with the deadline, and you don't shrink it. Being real means saying the thing at its actual size.

lines.text: “It's fine, we'll sort it.”
lines.outcome: She picks her plate up again. “Good, then,” and eats standing at the stove.
lines.why: Fine again. It shuts the door she just opened, and it leaves her eating alone in the same kitchen.

items.payoff: Tuesday, 8:40pm. Maya stops stirring and eats standing at the sink, alone. The rice goes cold on the back burner.
items.example:
Chemist shop, by the station, 7:30pm.
Pharmacist: “Are you feeling okay? Tell me the truth.”
You: “Not really. I've got a cough that keeps me up.”

items.title: Sunday, 9:30pm, the balcony
items.setting: Mum calls from 600 km away, the way she does on the ten-minute mark of your evening. A tap is running in the background at her end.

beats.text: “Are you eating properly? Tell me the truth, not the thing you say.”
beats.cue: her voice at the edge of worry, the tap still running

lines.text: “Yes, Mum, I eat every day. Don't worry.”
lines.outcome: Mum says “Good, good,” and then asks about the rent again, which means she heard the gap in your voice.
lines.why: This is the script: the reassurance that closes the call on the worry. It sounds loving, and it leaves her with a number she can't check.

lines.text: “Not always. When the deadlines close in, I skip lunch, and I'm scared the money won't stretch. I didn't want you to worry.”
lines.outcome: There is a long pause. Then Mum says she'd rather know the days you skip, so she can call you at lunch.
lines.why: This is being real: plain candour with no game in it. You don't have to sound strong for the call, and she can hear where you actually are.

lines.text: “You always do this. Dad was the same, and now you want me to worry about you too.”
lines.outcome: The scene stops there. Mum says “Fine,” and ends the call before you can answer.
lines.why: This turns her worry into a charge against Dad and against you. The real question disappears under the old story.

beats.text: “Then what do you want from me? Tell me what you need.”
beats.cue: the tap goes off at her end

lines.text: “I want you to ask how I am, and then wait for the real answer.”
lines.outcome: Mum goes quiet, then asks, “How are you, then?” and waits.
lines.why: You say what you want, plainly, without asking her to fix your life. That is a real request for company, not a rescue.

lines.text: “Don't worry about it, Mum. It'll sort itself out.”
lines.outcome: She sighs and says Dad would have said the same. The call drifts off to the building society.
lines.why: This is the scripted close. It takes the need off the table and tells her the real thing isn't wanted.

beats.text: “Tell me about your week, then. I never get to hear it.”
beats.cue: the kettle starting at her end

lines.text: “The orange was sour, Mum. Gran made me laugh about the stall. Next time I'll call you from the balcony when it's quiet.”
lines.outcome: Mum laughs, properly, for the first time in the call. “Balcony, then. Ring me on Sunday.”
lines.why: You offer a small, true detail from your week, which is a real gift to her. It doesn't need to be a confession to count as intimacy.

lines.text: “Work's fine. Nothing to tell.”
lines.outcome: She says “Okay,” in the voice that means it isn't okay, and the call ends on the building society.
lines.why: This is the scripted close. It leaves her with the sense of a door shut, which is exactly what she was afraid of.

items.payoff: Sunday, 9:45pm. Mum says “Fine” and ends the call. In the morning she sends a photo of the kitchen calendar, with the holiday weekend circled and nothing else written on it.
items.example:
Gym, by the bus stop, Saturday.
Trainer: “Are you doing the reps, or just standing there?”
You: “Standing. My shoulder's sore, and I didn't want to say so.”
Trainer: “Good. Then we do the easy set.”

rounds.label: Analyse, explain it
rounds.intro: Name the part that was missing from that reply. Then sort three more moments.

items.text: “Did you eat? Don't say fine.” You said fine anyway, though you knew you hadn't eaten, and the kitchen went quiet.
items.cue: the spoon still in her hand
options: Intimacy. You said too much to Maya, and the line handed her a weight she didn't need.
Spontaneity. 'Fine' was the reply you were taught for that question. The books call the freedom to choose and show a feeling from all your voices spontaneity, and you didn't use it.
Awareness. You didn't hear her question, so the reply came out of nowhere.
items.why: You knew you hadn't eaten, so awareness was working. The word 'fine' arrived without a choice, straight from what you were taught. Choosing a feeling from all your voices, instead of only the taught one, is spontaneity.

traps.0: Intimacy. You didn't say too much, since the line gave her almost nothing. Candour does come into it, but a candid reply starts with picking a feeling to show, and 'fine' was never picked.
traps.2: Awareness. You heard the question and you knew the answer. The gap was in the reply you gave after that.

items.example:
Dance class, Wednesday, 6:00pm.
Teacher: “How's your week? Don't say fine.”
Student: “Fine.”
Teacher: “Right, see you Friday, then.”

items.prompt: Three more moments, each with one capacity missing. Put each in the bin for the one that was missing.

items.text: “I walked home rehearsing what to say to Daniel on Monday. The rain had stopped, and I never saw it.”
items.why: Body on the pavement, mind in Monday's meeting. Berne's test for awareness is where your mind is while your body is here.

items.text: “Gran handed me the orange and I said ‘You shouldn't have’, same as always, though I was pleased and curious.”
items.why: Only the taught reply was on offer. Spontaneity is having the whole range of feelings to choose from, and here one rehearsed line covered all of them.

items.text: “I told Mum I was fine, then dropped hints about the bank, hoping she would offer to pay.”
items.why: The hints are a hook. Intimacy is candour with no game in it, and a hint is the opposite of asking plainly.

items.example:
Station platform, 8:05am.
Colleague: “Everything all right?”
You, eyes on your phone: “Fine.”
You are three stops past the one where you meant to get off.

debrief.nadia: You had all three this afternoon and lost one of them by evening, which is how it goes. The orange was real while you held it. The word 'fine' to your mother was not, and she heard the gap before you did. Nobody keeps all three running at once, all day. The only practice going is catching the old line before it leaves your mouth, and sometimes just after.
debrief.bookNote: The books call these awareness, spontaneity and intimacy, the three capacities of autonomy. Berne adds that overthrowing the old ways is never final, so you keep winning them back.

reflection.prompt: Where did you give the scripted reply this week when a fresh one was right there? What is actually stopping you from giving the fresh one next time?
